title: Malaysia Clamps Down on Fast Hiking Trend
paragraphs: Malaysia is making its hiking rules stricter as social media trends push people to take dangerous risks in the country's mountains.
As rescues increase, the government is especially worried about "compressed hikes," in which people try to do routes that normally take several days in just one day.
Some hikers try to do this with as little equipment as possible, hoping to make viral social media videos.

Earlier this year, local mountain guide Norimah Abd Karim told Malaysian news website Bernama that there are hikers who focus so much on "getting interesting content that they are willing to take risks and neglect their own safety."
The Fire & Rescue Department of Malaysia said the country had 52 cases of lost hikers in the first five months of 2026. That's 30% more than over the same period last year.

According to New Straits Times, one case included a group of 10 people getting lost at Bukit Kiara Federal Park in Kuala Lumpur in May. In another case, seven people got lost on Gunung Yong Belar mountain in February.

Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohammad from the Fire & Rescue Department said, "The public should not take safety lightly. Physical preparation and basic knowledge are very important to prevent unwanted incidents, including getting lost in the forest."

The government has said that certified guides will now be required for hikes in 189 high-risk locations, while pre-climb screening will be stronger, including requirements for health checks and insurance.
Malaysia has around 2,300 certified local guides trained to get people through hikes safely.

The forestry department for Perak state, home to the 130 million-year-old Belum Temengor rainforest, has also banned compressed hikes. Selangor, the state that surrounds Kuala Lumpur, has also suspended applications for them.
The exact new rules will depend on the route, so people should check before they climb.
